units.text: Amazon OpenSearch Service is a managed search and analytics engine. It helps people find relevant information without making the application search its entire database for every request. Imagine typing trail backpack into a shop's search box. The product database holds the original records, including the names and details of the products.

The shop copies the fields people should be able to search into an OpenSearch index. The index organizes that copy so it can find the words trail and backpack and return relevant matches. The index can lag behind the database if an update hasn't reached it yet. Use search to find a product, then rely on its authoritative record when the exact current information matters.

Amazon CloudWatch Logs collects application and A W S service logs so you can investigate what happened and when. Imagine a checkout app reporting a timeout. The log group brings the app's logs together, while each stream identifies the instance that sent its entries in this example. Both streams show a timeout at ten twenty-four. These are two recorded occurrences, one from each instance.

Search the logs around that time and compare the entries before drawing conclusions. If you configure a metric filter, it can count matching errors. An alarm on that metric can notify you when the count meets its condition. If another system needs the events, a subscription can forward them. Search for the cause, measure the pattern, or forward the events as needed.

Amazon DocumentDB is a managed document database with MongoDB compatibility. It is useful when an application often reads a group of related fields together. Take Maya's profile. When the app opens it, it needs her name, city, and interests. Those fields fit together in one document rather than being assembled from several unrelated records.

The document can hold an address inside the profile, and the interests can be stored as a list. The example shows the data in a familiar Jason-like form. Compatibility does not mean identical behavior. Before moving a MongoDB application, verify that its driver, queries, and features are supported. Test the operations your app really uses, not just whether it can connect.

Amazon Timestream is for measurements that make sense when you know when they were taken. It helps you look at how something changes over time, rather than just the latest value. Imagine a room sensor sending a temperature every few minutes. Each dot is one measurement paired with its timestamp. That makes it possible to ask what the temperature was at a particular time. Now look at the fifteen-minute averages.

They smooth out individual fluctuations and make the overall rise and fall easier to see. Use the original readings when the exact spikes matter. For a new workload, A W S recommends evaluating Timestream for InfluxDB. Timestream for LiveAnalytics is closed to new customers, while existing customers can keep using it.
